claim: Following the requirement to stop, there was an increase of right frontal beta (~13 to 30 Hz) at ~120 ms, likely a proxy of right inferior frontal gyrus.
source: We show that, following the requirement to stop, there was an increase of right frontal beta (~13 to 30 Hz) at ~120 ms, likely a proxy of right inferior frontal gyrus
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, and it is supported by data from Studies 4 and 5 showing beta bursts at ~120 ms.

claim: At 140 ms after the stop signal, there was a broad skeletomotor suppression, likely reflecting the impact of the subthalamic nucleus on basal ganglia output.
source: then, at 140 ms, there was a broad skeletomotor suppression, likely reflecting the impact of the subthalamic nucleus on basal ganglia output
evidence: Study 3 TMS data shows global motor suppression beginning at ~140 ms after the Stop signal.

claim: At ~160 ms after the stop signal, suppression was detected in the muscle.
source: then, at ~160 ms, suppression was detected in the muscle
evidence: Studies 1 and 2 show CancelTime (EMG decline) at ~160 ms after the Stop signal.

claim: The behavioral time of stopping (SSRT) was ~220 ms.
source: finally, the behavioral time of stopping was ~220 ms
evidence: SSRTBeh values across all studies ranged from 204-219 ms, as shown in Table 1.

claim: Response inhibition is a prefrontal (top-down) stopping of initiated response tendencies.
source: one important process is response inhibition – the prefrontal (top-down) stopping of initiated response tendencies (Aron, 2007)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Aron, 2007.

claim: Stop Signal Reaction Time (SSRT) is typically 200–250 ms in healthy adults.
source: the latency of stopping known as Stop Signal Reaction Time (SSRT), which is typically 200–250 ms in healthy adults (Verbruggen et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Verbruggen et al., 2019.

claim: SSRT is often longer for patients vs. controls in neuropsychiatric conditions.
source: SSRT has been useful in neuropsychiatry where it is often longer for patients vs. controls (Alderson et al., 2007; Bari and Robbins, 2013; Lavagnino et al., 2016; Lijffijt et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2014; Snyder et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The relation between SSRT and 'real-world' self-reported impulsivity is often weak.
source: a puzzle is that the relation between SSRT and 'real-world' self-reported impulsivity is often weak (Chowdhury et al., 2017; Enkavi et al., 2019; Friedman and Miyake, 2004; Lijffijt et al., 2004; McLaughlin et al., 2016; Skippen et al., 2019b)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Standard calculations of SSRT may overestimate the brain's stopping latency by ~100 ms.
source: recent mathematical modelling of behavior during the stop-signal task suggests that standard calculations of SSRT may overestimate the brain's stopping latency by ~100 ms (Skippen et al., 2019b; also see Bissett and Poldrack, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent modeling studies.

claim: EMG recordings revealed a decline in EMG activity at ~150 ms after the Stop signal, which is 50 ms before the SSRT of 200 ms.
source: in a recent study (Raud and Huster, 2017), electromyographic (EMG) recordings revealed an initial increase in EMG activity in response to the Go cue, followed by a sudden decline at ~150 ms after the Stop signal. This decline in EMG could be because of the Stop process 'kicking in' to cancel motor output – but the striking thing is that this was 50 ms before the SSRT of 200 ms.
evidence: This is based on a citation to Raud and Huster, 2017.

claim: The motor evoked potential (MEP) in the muscle that was-to-be-stopped reduced at ~150 ms.
source: The MEP in the muscle that was-to-be-stopped reduced at ~150 ms (Coxon et al., 2006; van den Wildenberg et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to TMS studies.

claim: There is 'global suppression' of corticospinal activity at ~150 ms for muscles not needed for the task.
source: other studies that measured the MEP from muscles that were not needed for the task, show there is 'global suppression' also at ~150 ms (Badry et al., 2009; Cai et al., 2012; Wessel et al., 2013a; Wessel and Aron, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous TMS studies.

claim: Global MEP suppression has been linked to activation of the subthalamic nucleus of the basal-ganglia.
source: This 'global MEP suppression' has been linked to activation of the subthalamic nucleus of the basal-ganglia (Wessel et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wessel et al., 2016.

claim: Successful stopping elicits increased beta band power over right frontal cortex in the time period between the Stop signal and SSRT.
source: in electrocorticography, electroencephalography (EEG), and magnetoencephalography (MEG) studies, successful stopping elicits increased beta band power over right frontal cortex in the time period between the Stop signal and SSRT (Castiglione et al., 2019; Schaum et al., 2020; Swann et al., 2009; Wagner et al., 2018; Wessel et al., 2013b)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous neurophysiological studies.

claim: On 53 ± 6% of Successful Stop trials there was a small but detectible EMG response (Partial EMG trials) in Study 1.
source: On 53 ± 6% of Successful Stop trials (i.e. where no keypress was made) there was a small but detectible EMG response (Partial EMG trials
evidence: This is a direct report of data from Study 1.

claim: The amplitude of EMG responses in the Partial EMG trials was 48 ± 3% smaller than in trials with a keypress in Study 1.
source: The amplitude of EMG responses (mean peak EMG voltage) in the Partial EMG trials was 48 ± 3% smaller than in trials with a keypress (Figure 2a)
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Mean CancelTime in Study 1 was 152 ± 11 ms.
source: study 1: mean CancelTime = 152 ± 11 ms
evidence: This is a direct report of data from Study 1.

claim: Mean SSRTBeh in Study 1 was 216 ± 8 ms.
source: mean SSRTBeh = 216 ± 8 ms
evidence: This is a direct report of data from Study 1.

claim: CancelTime was positively correlated with SSRTBeh in Study 1 (r = 0.71, p=0.020, BF10 = 3.6).
source: across participants, CancelTime was positively correlated with SSRTBeh (Figure 2d; study 1: mean CancelTime = 152 ± 11 ms, mean SSRTBeh = 216 ± 8 ms; r = 0.71, p=0.020, BF10 = 3.6)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis from Study 1, shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Partial EMG responses occurred on 49 ± 2% of Successful Stop trials in Study 2.
source: we observed partial EMG responses on 49 ± 2% of Successful Stop trials
evidence: This is a direct report of data from Study 2.

claim: The EMG amplitude in Partial EMG trials was 54 ± 1% smaller than the amplitude in trials with a keypress in Study 2.
source: where the EMG amplitude was 54 ± 1% smaller than the amplitude in trials with a keypress (Figure 2b)
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Mean CancelTime in Study 2 was 146 ± 4 ms.
source: mean CancelTime = 146 ± 4 ms
evidence: This is a direct report of data from Study 2.

claim: Mean SSRTBeh in Study 2 was 204 ± 4 ms.
source: mean SSRTBeh = 204 ± 4 ms
evidence: This is a direct report of data from Study 2.

evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis from Study 2, shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Mean CancelTime (147±5 ms) was 60±3 ms shorter than SSRTBeh in pooled studies 1 and 2.

evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis from pooled Studies 1 and 2.

claim: The difference between SSRTBeh and CancelTime is due to an inherent 'ballistic stage' in movements.
source: We hypothesized that the difference between SSRTBeh and the time of EMG cancellation (CancelTime) is due to an inherent "ballistic stage" in movements and once the muscle activity crosses the point-of-no-return they can no longer be stopped and a movement is inevitable (de Jong et al., 1990; Mirabella et al., 2006; Osman et al., 1986; Verbruggen and Logan, 2009)
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors, supported by citations to previous research on ballistic stages.

claim: The duration of ballistic stages has been estimated to be ~15 ms in saccades in non-human primates.
source: The duration of such ballistic stages has been estimated to be ~15 ms in saccades in non-human primates (Boucher et al., 2007; Kornylo et al., 2003; Purcell et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The duration of ballistic stages has been estimated to be ~50 ms for reaching movements in humans.
source: ~50 ms for reaching movements in humans (Gopal and Murthy, 2016; Jana and Murthy, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: SSRTEMG (157±7 ms) was significantly faster than SSRTBeh (207±3 ms) in pooled studies 1 and 2.
source: Pairwise comparisons showed that SSRTEMG (157±7 ms) was significantly faster than SSRTBeh (207±3 ms) (Figure 3b; t(41) = 8.2, pBon < 0.001, d = 1.3, BF10 > 100)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis from pooled Studies 1 and 2, shown in Figure 3b.

claim: SSRTEMG was not significantly different from mean CancelTime in pooled studies 1 and 2.
source: but importantly, not significantly different from mean CancelTime (t(41) = 1.5, pBon = 0.270, d = 0.2, BF10 = 0.5)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis from pooled Studies 1 and 2.

claim: The EMG response in the Partial EMG trials diverged from Correct Go and Failed Stop trials ~55 ms after EMG onset.
source: the EMG response in the Partial EMG trials (when aligned to the EMG onset) had a profile similar to the EMG response in the Correct Go and Failed Stop trials, but diverged ~55 ms after EMG onset (55 ms compared to Correct Go, and 56 ms compared to Failed Stop trials, Figure 3c)
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Mean CancelTime was positively correlated with the mean SSRTBEESTS (r = 0.54, p<0.001, BF10 > 100).
source: Across participants, mean CancelTime was positively correlated with the mean SSRTBEESTS (205 ± 3 ms; r = 0.54, p<0.001, BF10 > 100; Figure 3d)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis, shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The SD of CancelTime (33 ± 2 ms) was positively correlated with the SD of SSRTBEESTS (48 ± 5 ms; r = 0.42, p=0.005, BF10 = 6.9).
source: the SD of CancelTime (33 ± 2 ms) was positively correlated with the SD of SSRTBEESTS (48 ± 5 ms; r = 0.42, p=0.005, BF10 = 6.9; Figure 3e)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis, shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The percentage of trigger failures (4 ± 1%) was positively correlated with mean CancelTime (ρ = 0.57, p<0.001, BF10 > 100).
source: the percentage of trigger failures (4 ± 1%) was positive correlated with mean CancelTime (ρ = 0.57, p<0.001, BF10 > 100)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis.

claim: Global motor system suppression begins at 140 ms after the Stop-signal in Study 3.
source: Global motor system suppression begins at 140 ms after the Stop-signal, and thus ~20 ms prior to the mean CancelTime
evidence: This is directly stated based on TMS data from Study 3.

claim: MEP amplitudes were significantly suppressed on Successful Stop trials at 140 ms after the Stop signal in Study 3.
source: However, MEP amplitudes were significantly suppressed on Successful Stop trials at 140 ms (t(16) = 4.1, pBon = 0.003, BF10 = 39.8) and 180 ms (t(16) = 4.4, pBon < 0.001, BF10 = 65.2) after the Stop signal
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis from Study 3.

claim: The corticospinal conduction time was 23 ± 0.3 ms in Study 3.
source: This was 23 ± 0.3 ms
evidence: This is a direct report of data from Study 3.

claim: The suppression of MEPs in Successful Stop trials compared to Correct Go trials began in the 30 ms prior to the EMG decline in Study 3.
source: The suppression of MEPs in Successful Stop trials compared to Correct Go trials began in the 30 ms prior to the EMG decline (−30 to 0 ms: Z = 3.12, pBon = 0.005; 0 to 30 ms: Z = 4.48, pBon <0.001; 30 to 60 ms: Z = 2.45, pBon = 0.045)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis from Study 3.

claim: Burst % increased for Successful Stop trials (14.6 ± 1.7%) compared to baseline (9.9 ± 1.7%) in Study 4.
source: Post hoc t-tests showed that in the StopWin there was a significant increase in burst % for Successful Stop (14.6 ± 1.7%) compared to both its baseline (9.9 ± 1.7%; t(10) = 3.3, pBon = 0.022, BF10 = 7.6)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis from Study 4.

claim: Burst % increased for Successful Stop trials compared to Correct Go (9.6 ± 1.3%) in Study 4.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis from Study 4.

source: Across participants, the mean BurstTime (115 ± 6 ms) was significantly shorter than mean CancelTime (169 ± 10 ms; t(10) = 8.2, p<0.001, BF10 > 100)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis from Study 4.

claim: There was a strong positive relationship between BurstTime and CancelTime in Study 4 (ρ = 0.76, p=0.006, BF10 = 10.6).
source: and there was also a strong positive relationship between them (ρ = 0.76, p=0.006, BF10 = 10.6; Figure 5d

evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis from Study 5.

claim: Burst % was greater for Successful Stop compared to Correct Go (12.0 ± 1.4%) in Study 5.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis from Study 5.

claim: There was a significant positive relationship between BurstTime and CancelTime in Study 5 (ρ = 0.57, p=0.045, BF10 = 1.9).
source: and there was a significant positive relationship (ρ = 0.57, p=0.045, BF10 = 1.9; Figure 5d)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis from Study 5, shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Combining data from studies 4 and 5 confirms the strong relationship between right frontal beta BurstTime and CancelTime (ρ = 0.66, p<0.001, BF10 = 29.4).
source: Combining data from studies 4 and 5 confirms the strong relationship between right frontal beta BurstTime and CancelTime (ρ = 0.66, p<0.001, BF10 = 29.4)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis from pooled Studies 4 and 5.

claim: CancelTime reflects a trial-by-trial measure of the time of implementation of the Stop process.
source: These relationships between CancelTime and model estimates give further credence to our interpretation that CancelTime on Partial EMG trials reflects a single-trial measure of the time of implementation of the Stop process
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the correlations between CancelTime and BEESTS model estimates.

claim: The partial EMG activity represents a muscle manifestation of the stopped response.
source: several lines of evidence strongly suggest it is a muscle manifestation of the stopped response
evidence: This is an interpretation based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: CancelTime coincided well with the timing of a putative basal ganglia-mediated global motor suppression.
source: our TMS experiment demonstrated that CancelTime coincided well with the timing of a putative basal ganglia-mediated global motor suppression (Badry et al., 2009; Cai et al., 2012; Wessel and Aron, 2013; Wessel et al., 2016; Wessel and Aron, 2013; Wessel and Aron, 2017)
evidence: This is based on the TMS data from Study 3 and citations to previous research.

claim: The smaller amplitude and earlier decline of the partial EMG activity on Successful Stop was due to an active suppression of motor output.
source: This implies that the smaller amplitude and earlier decline of the partial EMG activity on Successful Stop was due to an active suppression of motor output
evidence: This is an inference based on the TMS data showing global motor suppression coinciding with CancelTime.

claim: SSRTBeh includes not only CancelTime but an extra, and variable, 60 ms ballistic stage.
source: As we show, SSRTBeh includes not only CancelTime but an extra, and variable, 60 ms ballistic stage
evidence: This is based on the finding that CancelTime was ~60 ms shorter than SSRTBeh.

claim: CancelTime might be a better metric of the time of implementation of the Stop process than SSRTBeh.
source: This suggests that SSRTBeh might be protracted by a peripheral delay and that CancelTime might be a better metric of the time of implementation of the Stop process
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of SSRTEMG, CancelTime, and SSRTBeh.

claim: The brain's stopping latency is ~ 140 ms.
source: One important consequence of our observation that the brain's stopping latency is ~ 140 ms is that neural events that mediate stopping need to occur before this time
evidence: This is based on the TMS data showing global motor suppression at ~140 ms.

claim: Right frontal beta activity increased ~ 120 ms after the Stop signal on Successful Stop trials.
source: Indeed, we found that right frontal beta activity increased ~ 120 ms after the Stop signal on Successful Stop trials
evidence: This is based on the EEG data from Studies 4 and 5.

claim: Across participants, there was a strong positive relationship between mean BurstTime and mean CancelTime.
source: and also that, across participants, there was a strong positive relationship between mean BurstTime and mean CancelTime
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis from Studies 4 and 5.

claim: Following the Stop signal, the right PFC including the rIFC and the preSMA gets activated at ~120 ms.
source: Following the Stop signal, the right PFC including the rIFC and the preSMA gets activated at ~120 ms
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 6, summarizing the temporal model.

claim: The right PFC activates the STN of the basal ganglia.
source: These region/s activate (green connections) the STN of the basal ganglia
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 6, based on the temporal model and previous literature.

claim: The STN activates the globus pallidus interna which, via its inhibition on the motor regions of the thalamus, cuts down the 'drive' to the motor cortex.
source: This in turn activates the globus pallidus interna which, via its inhibition (red connection) on the motor regions of the thalamus, cuts down the 'drive' to the motor cortex
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 6, based on the temporal model and previous literature.

claim: The outcome is a global motor suppression at ~140 ms after the Stop signal.
source: Theoutcome is a global motor suppression at ~140 ms after the Stop signal
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 6, based on the TMS data from Study 3.

claim: This suppression is reflected in the hand muscle at ~160 ms which is measured as the CancelTime.
source: This suppression is reflected in the hand muscle at ~160 ms which is measured as the CancelTime
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 6, based on the EMG data from Studies 1 and 2.

claim: There is a delay of ~60 ms at the muscle level which gets added to the behavioral estimate of SSRT.
source: There is a delay of ~60 ms at the muscle level which gets added to the behavioral estimate of SSRT
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 6, based on the comparison of CancelTime and SSRTBeh.

claim: The onset latency of the TMS-evoked MEP is likely an under-estimate of the mean conduction time of all pathways involved in voluntary movement.
source: Note, however, that the onset latency of the TMS-evoked MEP is likely an under-estimate of the mean conduction time of all pathways involved in voluntary movement, because TMS is biased towards recruiting fast conducting corticospinal neurons with mono-synaptic connections to the spinal motorneurons (Day et al., 1989; Edgley et al., 1997)
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with citations to previous research.

claim: The mean latency at which changes in motor cortical output are observable as changes in EMG activity is probably longer than 23 ms by several milliseconds.
source: Therefore, the mean latency at which changes in motor cortical output are observable as changes in EMG activity is probably longer than 23 ms by several milliseconds
evidence: This is an inference based on the understanding that TMS-evoked MEP onset latency underestimates conduction time.

claim: MEPs were also suppressed in Failed Stop versus Correct Go trials, but at some delay relative to Successful Stops and the time of EMG cancellation.
source: We note too, that MEPs were also suppressed in Failed Stop versus Correct Go trials, but at some delay relative to Successful Stops and the time of EMG cancellation (Figure 4d)
evidence: This is based on the trial-by-trial analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Part of the reason for the failure to stop is that the Stop process is initiated/implemented later in Failed Stop trials.
source: This is consistent with the idea that the Stop process is initiated even in Failed Stop trials, and that part of the reason for the failure to stop is that the Stop process is initiated/implemented later in these trials (the other reason being that the Go process might have been completed particularly quickly)
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of delayed MEP suppression in Failed Stop trials.

claim: The burst % was quite low on Successful Stop trials (~15%).
source: We also acknowledge that the burst % was quite low on Successful Stop trials (~15%)
evidence: This is based on the EEG data from Studies 4 and 5.

claim: CancelTimes on trials with and without bursts were not different in Study 5.
source: and that CancelTimes on trials with and without bursts were not different (Study 5: CancelTimeWith Burst = 164 ± 9 ms; CancelTimeNo Burst = 165 ± 9 ms, t(12) = 0.6, p=0.58, d = 0.2, BF10 = 0.3
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis from Study 5.

claim: The poor signal-to-noise of EEG could explain the low burst %.
source: While this might indicate that bursts are not necessary or sufficient for action-stopping, we think that the poor signal-to-noise of EEG could explain the low burst %
evidence: This is speculation by the authors to explain the low burst %.

claim: Beta bursts on Go trials might have had a role in proactive slowing on Go trials.
source: or the bursts might have had a role in proactive slowing on Go trials (as the task, after all, required participants to prepare to stop their response)
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about the functional role of beta bursts on Go trials.

claim: A recent scalp EEG study focused on the spatial and temporal dynamics of beta bursts saw that burst probability increased for likely dorsomedial frontal cortex (electrode FCz) rather than right frontal cortex.
source: a recent scalp EEG study focused on the spatial and temporal dynamics of beta bursts (Wessel, 2020). That study saw that burst probability increased for likely dorsomedial frontal cortex (electrode FCz) rather than right frontal cortex, as we do
evidence: This is a comparison to a previous study by Wessel, 2020.

claim: The discrepancy between the current study and Wessel (2020) could be explained by the use of a spatial filter approach versus channel space analysis.
source: This discrepancy could be explained by our use of a spatial filter approach whereas that study analyzed the data in channel space
evidence: This is speculation by the authors to explain the discrepancy with Wessel, 2020.

claim: Wessel (2020) observed that bursts increased over bilateral sensorimotor cortex ~ 25 ms after the frontal area, which was interpreted as inhibition of the motor system.
source: A further observation of Wessel (2020) was that bursts increased over bilateral sensorimotor cortex ~ 25 ms after the frontal area; and this was interpreted as inhibition of the motor system
evidence: This is a description of findings from Wessel, 2020.

claim: The observation of a decrease in corticospinal excitability within ~ 20 ms of right frontal bursts fits with Wessel (2020)'s observation.
source: This fits our observation of a decrease in corticospinal excitability within ~ 20 ms of right frontal bursts
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to Wessel, 2020.

claim: The maximum CancelTime reflects the last point at which a Stop process can intervene to prevent responses.
source: We suggest that the maximum CancelTime reflects the last point at which a Stop process can intervene to prevent responses
evidence: This is an interpretation by the authors based on the ballistic stage hypothesis.

claim: CancelTime is an overestimation of the brain's stopping latency since it does not include the corticospinal conduction time.
source: We note that CancelTime (a muscle measurement) is an overestimation of the brain's stopping latency since it does not include the corticospinal conduction time, which we estimated as ~ 20 ms
evidence: This is an inference based on the corticospinal conduction time measurement.

claim: CancelTime does not include the stopping latencies of the No EMG trials, which presumably reflect the fastest stopping latencies.
source: and does not include the stopping latencies of the No EMG trials, which presumably reflect the fastest stopping latencies where the Stop process was fast enough to cancel the impending response before it reaches the muscle
evidence: This is an inference about the No EMG trials.

claim: Global motor suppression occurs at ~ 140 ms, which is ~ 20 ms less than CancelTime.
source: Indeed, our TMS results show that global motor suppression, which we take as the time at which motor areas of the brain are suppressed, is ~ 140 ms (which is ~ 20 ms less than CancelTime)
evidence: This is based on the TMS data from Study 3.

claim: Neural events that mediate stopping need to occur before 140 ms.
source: One important consequence of our observation that the brain's stopping latency is ~ 140 ms is that neural events that mediate stopping need to occur before this time
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the timing of global motor suppression.

claim: CancelTime narrows the time window for the causal manipulation of neural structures involved in action-stopping.
source: Thus, CancelTime narrows the time window for the causal manipulation of neural structures involved in action-stopping
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of CancelTime for future research.

claim: The timings in the temporal model are approximations that are dependent on a range of factors.
source: We acknowledge that the timings in this model are approximations that are dependent on a range of factors (such as averaging across participants, running different experiments, and the particular parameters of detection algorithms)
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of limitations by the authors.

claim: There is a striking convergence of timings across the current experiments and in other studies.
source: However, we note a striking convergence of timings across the current experiments and in other studies, for example CancelTime (Hannah et al., 2019; Raud et al., 2019; Raud and Huster, 2017), time of MEP suppression (Coxon et al., 2006; van den Wildenberg et al., 2010), corticospinal conduction time (Groppa et al., 2012; Hamada et al., 2013), BurstTimes (Hannah et al., 2019), and the ballistic stage (Gopal and Murthy, 2016; Jana and Murthy, 2018)
evidence: This is an observation by the authors with citations to supporting studies.

claim: The current results are compatible with the interactive race model which suggests that the Stop process begins late, but implementation is quick.
source: Second, our results are compatible with the interactive race model which suggests that the Stop process begins late, but implementation is quick (i.e. within the last 1/3th of the stopping latency) (Boucher et al., 2007)
evidence: This is an interpretation by the authors with a citation to Boucher et al., 2007.

claim: The current results are compatible with the BEESTS model insofar as they point to a trigger process that has a duration of about 80–120 ms.
source: Third, our results are also compatible with the BEESTS model insofar as they point to a trigger process that has a duration of about 80–120 ms (Bekker et al., 2005; Skippen et al., 2019a)
evidence: This is an interpretation by the authors with citations to Bekker et al., 2005 and Skippen et al., 2019a.

claim: CancelTime will be more sensitive than SSRTBeh in discriminating patients from controls.
source: We predict that CancelTime will be more sensitive than SSRTBeh
evidence: This is a prediction by the authors about clinical applications.

claim: Future studies can easily estimate within-subject variability in CancelTime, which will likely discriminate patients from controls.
source: Furthermore, future studies can easily estimate within-subject variability in CancelTime, which will likely discriminate patients from controls
evidence: This is a prediction by the authors about clinical applications.

claim: Future studies may show stronger correlations between CancelTime and self-report than that seen between SSRTBeh and self-report.
source: We expect that future studies may show stronger correlations between CancelTime and self-report than that seen between SSRTBeh and self-report (also see Skippen et al., 2019b)
evidence: This is a prediction by the authors with a citation to Skippen et al., 2019b.

claim: Right frontal beta burst time might correlate more tightly with self-report measures than SSRTBeh.
source: likewise we predict that right frontal beta burst time might also correlate more tightly with self-report measures
evidence: This is a prediction by the authors.
